source.title: DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning

candidates.name: Reinforcement learning for language models
candidates.summary: Optimizing a language model's outputs to maximize a reward signal through trial-and-error sampling, rather than imitating labeled examples. The model generates responses, receives rewards, and updates its policy.
candidates.evidence: the reasoning abilities of LLMs can be incentivized through pure reinforcement learning (RL)

candidates.name: Group relative policy optimization
candidates.summary: A policy-gradient algorithm that samples a group of outputs per prompt and computes each output's advantage by normalizing its reward against the group's mean and standard deviation, removing the need for a learned value model.
candidates.evidence: GRPO samples a group of outputs {o1, o2, · · · , oG} from the old policy

candidates.name: Proximal policy optimization
candidates.summary: A policy-gradient reinforcement learning algorithm that limits each update by clipping the probability ratio between new and old policies, typically using a learned value model and generalized advantage estimation.
candidates.evidence: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) (Schulman et al., 2017), which is widely used in the RL stage of LLMs

candidates.name: Rule-based reward
candidates.summary: A reward computed by deterministic programmatic checks, such as matching a final answer to ground truth, running test cases, or verifying format, rather than by a learned reward model.
candidates.evidence: we employ rule-based rewards to deliver precise feedback for data in mathematical, coding, and logical reasoning domains

candidates.name: Reward hacking
candidates.summary: When a policy exploits flaws or biases in a reward function to obtain high reward without achieving the intended goal.
candidates.evidence: neural reward models are susceptible to reward hacking during large-scale reinforcement learning

candidates.name: Chain-of-thought reasoning
candidates.summary: Having a language model produce intermediate reasoning steps before its final answer, which improves performance on complex tasks.
candidates.evidence: chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting

candidates.name: Supervised fine-tuning
candidates.summary: Further training a pre-trained model on curated input-output pairs with a supervised (cross-entropy) objective so that it imitates the desired responses.
candidates.evidence: we bypass the conventional supervised fine-tuning (SFT) phase before RL training

candidates.name: Knowledge distillation
candidates.summary: Training a smaller student model to reproduce the behavior of a larger teacher, here by fine-tuning on outputs generated by the teacher.
candidates.evidence: we adopt a model distillation approach, a well-established technique for efficient knowledge transfer

candidates.name: Rejection sampling
candidates.summary: Generating many candidate outputs and keeping only those that pass a filter, such as correctness or readability, to build a training set.
candidates.evidence: we apply rejection sampling and SFT once more

candidates.name: Emergent reasoning behavior
candidates.summary: Capabilities such as self-reflection, verification and strategy switching that appear during training without being explicitly taught.
candidates.evidence: facilitates the emergent development of advanced reasoning patterns, such as self-reflection, verification, and dynamic strategy adaptation

candidates.name: Test-time compute scaling
candidates.summary: Improving model performance by spending more computation at inference, for example by generating longer reasoning chains or sampling multiple answers.
candidates.evidence: scales test-time compute to solve challenging problems

candidates.name: Pass@k and majority voting
candidates.summary: Pass@k estimates the chance that at least one of k sampled answers is correct; majority voting (consensus, self-consistency) picks the most frequent answer among k samples.
candidates.evidence: self-consistency decoding (Wang et al., 2023c)

candidates.name: Kullback-Leibler divergence
candidates.summary: A measure of how one probability distribution differs from a reference distribution. In RL fine-tuning it is used as a penalty to keep the policy near a reference policy.
candidates.evidence: KL coefficient to 0.001

candidates.name: Advantage estimation
candidates.summary: The advantage measures how much better an action's outcome is than a baseline expectation; it is used to weight policy-gradient updates, often via a learned value function.
candidates.evidence: Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE)

candidates.name: Reward model
candidates.summary: A learned model that scores responses, typically trained on human or model preference data, to supply reward signals for RL.
candidates.evidence: we resort to reward models to capture human preferences in complex and nuanced scenarios

candidates.name: Process reward model
candidates.summary: A reward model that scores individual intermediate reasoning steps rather than only the final outcome.
candidates.evidence: Process Reward Model (PRM) PRM is a reasonable method to guide the model toward better approaches

candidates.name: Monte Carlo tree search
candidates.summary: A search algorithm that explores a decision tree by random simulations and value estimates, concentrating on promising branches.
candidates.evidence: we explored using Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to enhance test-time compute scalability

candidates.name: Mixture-of-experts
candidates.summary: A neural architecture in which a router activates only a subset of expert sub-networks per token, so total parameters greatly exceed those used per token.
candidates.evidence: Built on a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, DeepSeek V3 has 671 billion total parameters, with 37 billion activated per token

candidates.name: LLM-as-a-judge
candidates.summary: Using a language model to grade or compare other models' outputs, for example against a reference answer or in pairwise preference comparisons.
candidates.evidence: we employed the LLM-as-a-Judge approach, utilizing an advanced GPT version

candidates.name: Language consistency reward
candidates.summary: A reward term for the fraction of words in a chain of thought that are in the target language, used to discourage language mixing.
candidates.evidence: calculated as the proportion of target language words in the CoT

candidates.name: Benchmark data contamination
candidates.summary: Overlap between training data and evaluation sets that inflates scores; it is mitigated by filtering, such as removing texts sharing n-gram sequences with test questions.
candidates.evidence: filtered out any text segments ... that contained matching 10-gram sequences from evaluation questions

candidates.name: Jailbreak attack
candidates.summary: An adversarial prompt technique intended to circumvent a model's safety alignment and elicit harmful output.
candidates.evidence: R1 can be subject to jailbreak attacks

resolutions.name: Reinforcement learning for language models
resolutions.reason: It is RL applied to language models in general, which is a special case of reinforcement learning and broader than RLHF, so it matches none of the existing concepts.

resolutions.name: Pass@k and majority voting
resolutions.reason: It bundles two separate ideas, pass@k and majority voting, which the graph already holds as distinct nodes, so it is not the same as either one.

resolutions.name: Reward model
resolutions.reason: It is the general reward model concept, which is broader than the preference reward model (a specific type) and also covers process and generative reward models.
